utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Apologies of the Chamber for our late start. More than one matter delayed us. We are shortly to hear a witness in respect of whom there has been an application for protective measures, which was over the weekend, the application was supplemented with additional material. Good afternoon, Mr. Djordjevic. Do you wish to be heard in respect of this application for protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the reason that the Defence considers that this witness does not -- that his testimony does not warrant any protective measures is the fact that he had already testified before this Tribunal to the facts that he is going to testify about today as well. And if indeed there were threats directed at this witness, and I don't know from whom or where, and I assume that this would be something to discuss in closed session, we are, as a matter of course, against protective measures for this witness. Of course, that might change depending on the situation. As we proceed and if we hear any arguments that may sound sound enough for this witness to be questioned as a protected witness, the Defence might agree to that subsequently. For now, it is our position that it is unnecessary; and based on what I read from the application submitted by the Prosecution, the witness himself said that he was not willing to testify either by pseudonym or face and voice distortion. Regardless of any of those protective measures, everyone would be able to actually guess who the protected witness is, and therefore, for now I believe that there is no reason for any protective measures to be issued in respect of this witness. Of course, I assume that the witness will wish to hear -- that the Trial Chamber will wish to hear the witness as well and to hear his reasons for why he is seeking protective measures, and based on that, maybe then we will be able to make a qualified decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your submissions and their succinctness, Mr. Djordjevic. The Chamber, at the moment, is not minded to hear additional evidence, but understands clearly from your submission that you are opposed taking the position that there is not demonstrated a sufficient justification. Is there anything further, Mr. Stamp, that you would want to put in respect of this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that while the application is on the dividing line between sufficiently justified and not, the totality of the circumstances is sufficient to persuade the Chamber that there is, in the mind of the accused at least, a real threat and a serious threat, which is likely to be activated if he should repeat the evidence or something like the evidence which he previously gave and which led to an earlier threat to him. In these circumstances, the Chamber is persuaded that it should order protective measures. It recognizes, in view of the particular, even specific aspects of his evidence, that it would be quite readily possible to identify him simply by hearing the evidence, and in those circumstances, the Chamber is of the view that the appropriate protective measure should be for the evidence to be given in closed session. That will be the decision of the Chamber. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be very brief because it is not up to me to comment the decision of the Trial Chamber. I just wanted to intervene regarding the transcript. It says in the transcript whereas in the mind of the accused and the accused could be the witness or my own defendant here. So if you look at line 23 on page 2 it says "in the mind of the accused at least" so we need to direct this because what should stand there in fact is in the mind of the witness at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic, for identifying my error. I had intended to refer not to this present accused, but to the person who for -- to avoid confusion is better described as the intended witness. And it was intended by those comments to indicate that there is in his mind the Chamber accepts this concern which is genuine and that it therefore influences him in a way which satisfies the Chamber, according to the appropriate test that protective measures are justified. If the witness could be brought in. While that is occurring, I would mention that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the witness could be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we wait, Your Honour, would you allow me to address the Trial Chamber in a few words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you allow me first to deliver another oral decision, Mr. Djordjevic. Pending admission marked for identification are two documents tendered by the Prosecution. They are P97 and P102. Each of those are marked pending translation. Translations have now been received. They may be uplifted, the translations into the document in e-court, and will become exhibits rather than marked for identification. Now, Mr. Djordjevic, while you are speaking we will move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. You suggest now we have the second break, is that it, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will half an hour be timely for the witness to be here?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I see you on your feet, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As the lead counsel in these proceedings, I will like to request that the next witness be questioned by attorney Marie O'Leary in the cross-examination phase, and I hope that you will approve this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. We've had not only written advice from you in respect of Mr. Popovic, which we granted, but we've had a similarly framed advice in respect of Ms. O'Leary. And the Chamber is similarly prepared to grant that request. So we now have the benefit of hearing four counsel for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This is our desire and wish to allow our junior colleagues to join us and to become even better Defence counsel than they already have been so far. They both have a lot of experience, but this will certainly be helpful in their further work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. We will resume at I think at 5.40 just to be sure that the witness is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before we begin, we had a quick preliminary matter about the statement of this witness. In our motion opposing 92 ter as a mode of testimony for Mr. Fuat Haxhibeqiri. We had made an argument that part of the reasoning to keep out his statement was that it is somewhat confused in that he makes some conclusions and statements of others that's intermixed with his own eye-witness testimony. Additionally, he gives some opinions that are more appropriate, we feel, to an expert witness and not a fact witness. While we appreciate and do respect the Trial Chamber's decision in his mode of testimony, in doing further preparations for the cross-examine we would seek to have this 92 ter statement redacted to not include the summaries and the opinions, as they're not appropriate to the testimony of a fact witness in our opinion. In particular, we take opposition to pages 6 through 9 in the English pages of the statement which is 65 ter 2235, and specifically on page 6 of the English version when he starts with "From my investigation I have witnesses that say ..." until the dotted line. And also on page 7, then, of the English version when he says "In my position with the CDHRF, I have interviewed ..." which is just under the dotted line, which goes on until "... in 1998." On page 8. Furthermore, we take opposition to the last paragraph of the statement on page 9 in the English version that starts with "As a result of interviewing ..." These passages list -- were told to him, but they're lacking in detail sufficient for us to do any real cross-examine to get more details as we don't feel he has the information with him as it is not personal information to him. As we can't properly challenge the details of these events and primarily seek out the perpetrators that he is accusing in these statement passages, we would ask that these portions be stricken from the record as he has no personal knowledge. We understand that the Chamber may want to wait until his testimony is finished and analyse whether that is appropriate, but we would make the motion at this time, with hope to renew afterwards, if his testimony goes as we anticipate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. O'Leary. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is our position that the Chamber has already ruled on this matter. This is an issue that the Defence should have raised in their motion -- in their response to our motion to call this witness pursuant to 92 bis. And the Chamber's decision of 1st July, the Chamber stated that it decided to admit Mr. Haxhibeqiri's written statement, and we consider that this matter has already been ruled upon. It is also our view that the issues that my learned colleague is raising can be adequately examined when she questions the witness during her opportunity to cross-examine. So I do not believe that this is a matter that cannot be explored in cross-examination. The witness is being made available exactly for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. O'Leary, the Chamber is not of the view that it should take up this motion at this time. It has decided to receive the statement, recognising that aspects of it are perhaps not in the usual form. It will be apparent, though, to all that the persuasive force of some of the statement is less than would be the case were the witness speaking of his own personal observation and knowledge, and especially I speak there because of the generality of some of the things in parts of the statement. The Chamber will, in assessing what weight is appropriate to be given to different parts of the statement, take into account the matters I've just mentioned and will take into account the cross-examination of any that may be directed in respect of them. I think that is a sufficient indication of our position. If the witness could now be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Ms. Kravetz has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I'm Fuat Haxhibeqiri.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When and when were you born, Mr. Haxhibeqiri?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: I was born in Gjakove on the 24th of March, 1956.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in 1999, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: In Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where were you employed at the time in 1999?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: I was working for the private company Agimi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in addition to working for that company, did you conduct any other sort of activity? And I'm speaking specifically of the period of 1999.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. I was an activist within the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what sort of work did you carry out for the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms in Gjakove?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: We would collect information from the ground, information pertaining to cases of violations of human rights in our municipality committed by the Serb forces. In other words, we would go out on the ground, document the cases, and also collect information pertaining to such cases from people who would report them to our office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just very briefly, could you tell us how it was that you collected this information? What would you do to collect information to pertain to such cases?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: People would come to our office, tell us what had happened to him or her, show us photographs in case they had photographs that documented tortures committed by the police or army, and then we would forward this information to the head office in Prishtina by fax initially, and later on via telephone and other communication means. We would also go out on the ground to document such cases, and we would support this documentation with photographs in case there were photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, in August of 2001 did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecution in this Tribunal in relation to events you witnessed in your municipality and that you personally investigated?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, did you have the opportunity to go over your statement?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And having reviewed your statement, are you satisfied that the information contained within the statement is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this statement, the 65 ter 02235, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1068, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will now proceed to read the in-court summary for this witness. The witness is a resident of Hadum neighbourhood of Djakovica town. He was working for the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms in Djakovica in 1999. He describes the military buildup within the town from 1998 onwards and the positions of heavy weapons and barracks. On 23rd March, 1999, the witness went into hiding in the Blloku i Ri neighbourhood of the town after the offices of the witness's organisation were searched by police and staff arrested. In the early hours of 25th March, Serb forces arrived in the neighbourhood of Carshia e Madhe in the old town of Djakovica, and the witness saw property subsequently burning. On 26th March, 1999, properties were burned in the Blloku I Ri neighbourhood where he was hiding. He named six persons killed that night. On 2nd April, 1999 police evicted the occupants of the house where the witness was hiding. At that time, he took refuge in a drain in the back garden where he escaped detection. He remained there for four days. Having returned to his home address, he then witnessed a daily cycle of burning of Kosovo Albanian property by Serb forces. The witness quotes municipality figures for deaths, missing and displaced persons, and property destruction for 1998 and 1999. He details results of the investigations of his organisation into several deaths and expulsions within Djakovica town. That's the end of the in-court summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, I would like to ask you some questions in relation to your statement, and I would like to ask you to try to be as brief as possible in your answers so we can proceed efficiently today through my questions. I want to start by asking you questions about events that took place in March 1999 which you describe in your statement. In your statement, you say that on 23rd March, 1999, the offices of your organisation were searched and that staff was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is, for reference, at the bottom of page 5 of the English, and in the B/C/S version is page 6 on the top. I believe it's the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you say that after this happened, this search that went on in the organisation, you took shelter in the Blloku i Ri neighbourhood. Could you tell us exactly where you went in this neighbourhood to take shelter?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, Midjeni [phoen] Street. Gani Efendiu was the owner of the house where I took shelter. He was a doctor by profession.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was there anyone else in that house other than yourself, when you went to take shelter there?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. The owner himself, that is the doctor; his wife; and his two sons, students; and another neighbour with her two daughters who were also students. I was there with the eight members of my family.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You say that you were there with the eight members of your family. Are these eight members of your family other persons than the persons you've mentioned, or are you saying that the doctor and his wife and his family were related to you?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: The doctor's family is a relative of my mother. They are related to my mother's family.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why is it that you decided to go to that house for shelter? Why did you go to that house and that neighbourhood for shelter?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: When I heard that the office was surrounded, searched, and the personnel arrested, I decided to hide, to seek shelter in this house. A house of a relative of my mother.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is at page 6 in the English on the top, and it's also on page 6 of the B/C/S towards the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- you say that some days later, on the 26th of March, you saw six houses burning in the Blloku i Ri neighbourhood from where you were hiding and that these houses belonged to political activists. Can you tell us, when you say that you saw these houses burning from where you were hiding, exactly where were you at the time when you saw these houses burning?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: I was in the doctor's house, and from the second floor we could see the houses burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And would it have been houses located in the proximity or around the same area of where the doctor's house was, or were there --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, they were at about 60 to 100 or 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement that these houses belonged to political activists. Do you know what was the ethnicity of the persons to whom these houses belonged to?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: All of them were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in your statement -- and this is moving forward in time to the beginning of April 1999, you tell us that on 2nd April, two policemen in a blue vehicle came to the house where you were sheltering.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is, again, on page 6 of the English at the bottom, and in the B/C/S it's page 7, I believe it's the fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this -- you say it's in the house in Blloku i Ri where you were sheltering. And in your statement you indicate that these policemen ordered the persons to leave the house. Now, you've told us who all was in the house with you. After these policemen arrived, did the persons who were in the house with you leave the house?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: As they were threatened, they had to leave. I heard myself, when the police ordered them to leave the house, to go to the church and there there would be a bus waiting for them to send them to Albania. They ordered them to leave the car keys in the house, and made them walk in the direction I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether policemen went into the houses of any of the neighbours of the doctor at whose house you were staying, or did they only come to the house where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: They went to each and every house and threatened the owners of the house to throw grenades into their houses in case they refused to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what did the neighbours do after these persons went to their houses, do you know?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: All of them, all the residence of Blloku i Ri neighbourhood, had to leave in a short time. About 20.000 to 30.000 people from the town were ordered to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us that all of the residence of Blloku i Ri had to leave in a short time. How do you know that? Is this something you observed yourself or that you hear from others? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone during the days I remained there. I was hiding in a drain behind the doctor's house. I stayed there for four days, and I didn't see a single Albanian during those four days. I only saw policemen and their respective wives who would come in the evenings, loot the houses, load the cars and other vehicles with everything they could find in the abandoned houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You just told us earlier that about 20-, or 30.000 people had left or were ordered to leave the house and you explained that all the residence of the Blloku i Ri had left. How do you know that, that they had left? Did you see them leave, did someone tell you they left? How did you know they had left?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Well, it wouldn't take one to do much thinking when one hears such a threat, a threat that could blow up your house. Nobody would choose to remain in the house once they threatened to throw a hand-grenade into the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, on 2nd April, you are saying that all of the residences left because you believe that they would have -- they would have been -- would have obeyed the threat that was made to them; is that what you are saying? It's not --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There was a threat. We were not able to sleep. We were dressed at all times. We were at all times anticipating their arrival into our houses. We were expecting the worst to happen as it happened in many other cases in our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Why was it that you were expecting the arrival of these policemen? What sort of information did you have that made you believe that they would be arriving to your -- to the house where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Three days earlier, more than 100 people were killed. We had heard that these many people were killed in this neighbourhood, 20 here, 30 there, 30 in that village, and so forth. At that time, the land-line was still working and we were able to collect information from other neighbourhoods as to the number of people who had been killed and the number of houses that had been burned down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to go back to the 2nd of April, you've told us that these two policemen arrived to your house. Did you see any other policemen in the neighbourhood that day when these two policemen arrived to your house? The house where you were staying, I mean.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: One of them was a local policeman, an Albanian by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And other than this Albanian that you saw, did you see any other policemen or any other persons in uniform on the 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you remain in hiding for some days and that when you went out there were policemen everywhere. Where was it that you saw these policemen?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: On the streets.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can I ask you to be a bit more precise. Do you mean the streets in the neighbourhood where this house was or somewhere else in another neighbourhood? Where exactly was it that you saw these policemen?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: When I arrived in my house, that is after three or four days of stay in my hiding place, around the 5th of April I went back to my house, and there I could see policemen and paramilitaries passing by my gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say you arrived in your house, in which neighbourhood was this house when you arrived on the 5th of April?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: My house is in the Hadum neighbourhood in the old part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, when you left the doctor's house where you were staying, your relatives house in the Blloku i Ri neighbourhood, and went to your house in the Hadum neighbourhood, was the area where the doctor's house was located still inhabited by the neighbours? Were they still there in their houses, if you know?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Everybody had already left that neighbourhood. I saw some people on the way, and I told them that I had to leave that neighbourhood because I no longer felt safe there, that I had to go to my own house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who were these people that you met on the way that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Citizens of Gjakove. Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that on the 5th of April you returned to your house in the Hadum neighbourhood. And earlier you had told us how you had seen -- while you were still at the doctor's house you had seen some houses burning belonging to some political activists. When you went from the Blloku i Ri neighbourhood to the Hadum neighbourhood, did you see any other houses that had been damaged by fire?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. There I also saw houses that were damaged by fire. About 200 of them including some small businesses. These houses were set on fire on the 24th and the 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say that about 200 houses had been set on fire including --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Which neighbourhood are you speaking about were these houses and small businesses were located?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Hadum neighbourhood. Carshia e Vjeter also called. In other words, around my house, more than 15 shops were burned. My uncle's house, who is in the same courtyard with mine, was also burnt down; it was a new house. And at about 500 metres from my house, there were many other houses and small shops burned down, and I could see all of them with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is the Hadum neighbourhood in the old town of Djakovica, what is known as the old town?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. It is part of the old town. It is known as the old town. It is -- it has oriental architecture. It is a protected area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is there a mosque located in the old town of Djakovica, Mr. Haxhibeqiri?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, the mosque itself is called the Hadum mosque. It was built about 400 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you know -- were you able to pass by the mosque and see in what condition it was on the 5th of April?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. I passed by the mosque, and I could see it from my house because it is at 50 metres' aerial distance from my house. The auxiliary buildings of the mosque were also burnt down. And the mosque itself, the inside part was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were you able to obtain any information while you were there as to what had happened to the mosque, how it had been burnt down?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: No, there was no one I could ask at the time because people had already been expelled from the old town; they were made to go to Albania. As I said, there was no one there. There were only policemen. There was no witness as to the burning of the mosque. That same night, six persons were killed. They were killing people, expelling people, and burning buildings at the same time in the old neighbourhood. They were made to leave under threat. So the first killings occurred on the 24th of March. That is to say, on the 25th of March at 1.00 a.m. these activities began, the houses were being burnt by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I just want to clarify some of your answers, and we'll take it step by step. First of all, when I was asking you about whether you had you had seen any damage to houses. You spoke about 200 of them and -- including small businesses, and you said these houses were set on fire on the 24th and 25th of March. How do you know that? From where did you obtain this information?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: From my brothers. They had informed me by phone. They told me that the shop where I was working was also burnt down including other shops in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can you tell us something about who these shops belonged to, and I'm speaking about this --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: They belonged to Albanians. All of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What about the houses that you say were set on fire?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: They belonged to Albanians, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you said you obtained this information from your brother, your brothers. Where were they that they were able to know about this?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: They were at home when the houses were being set on fire. Once they saw that, they fled their homes and went to other safer neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you have also spoken about killings and you said that the killings began on the 23rd of March and then continued from then. How do you know this? Who told you that there were killings going on in Djakovica town?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: The killings began on the 24th of March immediately after the NATO bombing began at midnight or shortly after midnight. This was planned and organised killing, organised by the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, I'm sorry to interrupt you. What I'm asking is who told you about this? How did you obtain this information? Was it something you saw yourself? Did somebody speak to you about this?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: I was informed via telephone and also by the residents from that neighbourhood. That's how I learned about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say that you were informed by the residence from that neighbourhood, which neighbourhood are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: The residence of Hadum neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what did the residence of Hadum tell you was happening in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Three of them were friends of mine, and they lived just 30 to 50 metres away from my home, and three others. I heard down the phone line from people. They told me the names of the people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did they tell you how they obtained this information as to who had been killed in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Of course, when your brother tells you the names of the people who were killed, I knew that it was from a safe source. It was all witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, I understand from your statement that you stayed in your house until the end of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Ten days I stayed with my uncle in a different neighbourhood, Hanke [phoen] it's called. I stayed there for ten days because I ran out of food, so I went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And after those ten days, did you return to your house in the Hadum neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed there almost all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you have told us that you, when you returned to the Hadum neighbourhood, you observed some damage that had been done to the mosque. During the time that you were there until from the end of the war, was any additional damage done to the Hadum mosque that you were able to observe or witness?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. On the 7th or on the 8th, I'm not sure, I was in the courtyard of my house when the minaret of the mosque, because of what I believed was an internal explosion, collapsed. At that moment, I went up on the second floor and from the roof I was following the developments; and within five a minutes the minaret collapsed, and I saw no one there. Whereas the mosque itself was damaged, half of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were you able to obtain any information as to how -- who had caused this damage to the minaret of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: No, because that was on the 7th of May when there was fighting in the Cabrat hill which is on the west side of the town. There was fighting between the KLA and the Serb forces. And as a consequence of the fighting, more than 100 people were killed. About 100 houses were burned down. And more than 300 people were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is the Cabrat hill located in the proximity of the mosque, or is it in a different area of the town?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: It's not far. From my house it's as the crow flies about 300 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how did you know that these persons were killed in this fighting?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Three of those killed and two of those arrested were sons of my uncle; I'm talking about those three killed. And two of those arrested include my brother, and the son of my uncle was also arrested on the street. They were expelled from the houses where they were staying. And those who were not separated from the column of the people, obviously the elderly, they continued in the direction of Albania. But the younger people were arrested in front of the municipality assembly hall. And there were more than 300 people who were taken to the suburbs of the city. They were inside a carpenter's shop, and they were held there for about 6 days. 155 of the 300 ended up in the prison of Peja. For six days, they were given no food, or they were given insufficient food. It is just two slices of bread for 36 hours, and they gave no water to them or gave them very little water, which was not enough. And when they were weakened after those 6 days, they were taken to Peja prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to have Exhibit P823 up on the screen. And this is a map --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to continue with what I was saying for another 30 seconds, if I may. Just to complete the picture. And from the prison of Peja, they were moved to the prison of Dubrava. 26 of the 155 who were detained, they were killed, they were shot, with the exception of two who died because of the bombing. The rest were executed by the personnel of the Dubrava prison by the Serb prison wardens.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, I'm going to stop you there just because we have very limited time. I know you have a lot of information to give the court, but your statement is already before the Chamber and unfortunately we can't explore each one of these instances.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have P823 up on the screen, and I want page 29. This is a map of Djakovica town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't got the map up yet on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I would like to stay in the bottom half of the map, if we can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to please assist the witness in making markings on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, I want you to make a couple of markings on this map. We see at the bottom of the map -- do you have the map before you?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see at the bottom the map a Roman numeral VII, and it's marked Blloku i Ri. Is this the area where you say you were hiding?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you just -- I know the map is not very detailed, but could you mark, approximately, the area where it is that you were staying during the events that you've described with an X. If you can draw --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If the usher could kindly assist the witness to --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Midjeni Street is this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You can draw on the screen.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you saw six houses that were burned that belonged to political activists. Could you just draw a circle to indicate the area where it is that these houses were burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the record, the witness has marked an X where the house -- the doctor's house was. For the sake of the record, the witness has drawn a larger dot to the top right of where the X was to indicate the area where the houses were burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you returned to the Hadum neighbourhood on the 5th of April. Do we see that up on the screen here? If you can just draw a circle around where that neighbour is located.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you just draw a bigger circle so we know which area we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you saw shops that were burned down and houses that were burned. Where exactly in this area were the shops and the houses that you saw had been burned? If you are able to tell on this map.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: If this is the mosque, my house should be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you draw a number 1 there where your house is located.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you mentioned the mosque. Can you draw a number 2 to indicate where the mosque was located.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: If it's this one, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, the shops and businesses that you spoke -- the houses and shops that you spoke about, where are they located in relation to your house?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: If the road is this one, then all those were along this road. It continues up to here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We can't see anything unless you mark it on the map, sir. So if you could just draw a line to indicate the road.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: The road is in red actually, but I'll do it. It continues further down from the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you're saying that the shops and houses you saw were along this road that you've marked in red?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, on both sides of the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The witness has drawn a line across the area that he has circled as being the Hadum neighbourhood to indicate the road along which he saw shops and business -- and houses burned down. Your Honours, I wonder if we could have this map admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1069, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The road is named after Ishmajl Qamali [phoen], so it's Ishmajl Qamali road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examination by Ms. O'Leary

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. My name is Marie O'Leary, I'm representing the Defence of Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic this evening. With me is our lead counsel Mr. Dragoljub Djordjevic and Mr. Aleksandar Popovic. Now, I've been over your statement, so I have a couple of questions to just clarify some matters. First of all, I want to learn a little bit more about the Council for Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms in Gjakove. I tried to visit the site, but it appeared to be under construction at the moment. But it still is a functioning organisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No. When --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Please. Time after time when there are projects, projects to be involved with, we do get involved; but the nature of the work that we were involved in has dropped down and the interest has decreased somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you are now --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: The nature of the work has changed, so it's not as it used to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you are now engaged on a more sporadic basis, as needed?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when was -- I'm going to refer to it as the CDHRF. When was that founded?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you a part of founding this organisation?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: No. I started sometime during the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you were involved with the organisation primarily from 1995 to 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you were chairman of the CDHRF for three years, 1998 to 2001?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: To start with, I wasn't; but after the war, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How did you come about this position? Is there an election of the members, or is it volunteer?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: It was an election. I was elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how many members were there at approximately that time?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you still active with the CDHRF when needed?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: The central headquarters in Pristina, when they get a project, for example, the general election, so we are engaged for the duration of the two months into and up to the election. In that case, I would call on the staff, and, of course, this is on specific projects. Because otherwise, I'm involved with my own things. Now, we mainly are engaged when there are elections. At a national level.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who determines what projects you will be involved in, what you'll take on?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: It's the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms in Prishtina. We are a sub-council.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could have your statement up on our screen so you can see --

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Which is now P1068. Going to page 2 in the English version, I believe it's also 2 in the Albanian version; 5 in e-court in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to talk a little bit about the goals that you've talked about of the organisation, particularly in 1998 and 1999. And if I'm reading in the English while we wait for a second the Albanian should pop up on the left, but you're saying in paragraph 3 of the English: "Part of the aims of the organisation is to collect evidence, data, and information of abuses of human rights." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And is that -- and you'll have it on your screen on the left there if it's a little bit easier to refer to. But was that abuses at that time of Albanian citizens or it is all ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Only Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If that was part of the goal of the organisation, you said part of the aims, what were the other aims beyond collecting evidence, data, and information of abuses? What else did you engage in in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: The main activity was collecting the correct information about the violation of human rights that was taking place in our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to clarify, from your prior statement, just a few lines before, that would be just the abuses against the human rights of the Albanian citizens; correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. Only the human rights of the Albanians because it was only the Albanians who reported these violations. We didn't receive reports of violations from other ethnicities. Partly from the Roma, although it was a minor proportion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Then I want to talk a little bit more about the interviews and how they were conducted. First of all, these were done in conjunction with the ICG; correct? The statements that were taken?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: No, this statement was taken from the international Tribunal here at the Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Correct. Sorry if I jumped ahead a little bit there, but in this statement here actually -- MS. MARIE O'LEARY: At page 7 of the English, if we could go to that, and again at page 9; but if we could look at page 7 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You state that as a result of interviewing over 1.000 people in Gjakove, you had done some interviews, I believe, with the International Crisis Group, I think it is, your organisation had, and you had participated personally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in stating that you interviewed over 1.000 people in Gjakove, you actually only personally interviewed about 100 people; correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: That's correct. There were about 10 or 11 of us who were interviewing people, and each one of us interviewed people in our respective areas, covering villages or neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "respective areas" do you mean geographically or professionally?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Geographically.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this was done all over Kosovo or just in the Djakovica municipality?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: It relates only to Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So in this 1.000 interviews that were taken in the Gjakove municipality, you said at some point you had read through them or you were familiar with the information contained in the other 900 statements?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you reviewing them for anything specific, or was it just to compile further reports for your organisation that you went over the other 900?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: To have information about what was going on across the municipality. To get all the statistics, the numbers of those killed, those arrested, and detained, because the crimes were not evidenced. Some of them still are unknown and remain a mystery. Because there were people -- corpses being brought from Batajnica, and to this day we still have people who are missing and we don't know their whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say - and to go back a couple of lines here - you say "those arrested, and detained," are you speaking about Albanians who were arrested and detained, or are you speaking of Serbs who were arrested and detained?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: We are talking about Albanians only, because if you were Albanian, you were persecuted, you were beaten up, you were killed, and everything -- the worst happened to you because you were Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you do any research or interviewing about those arrested and detained Serbs who may have been perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: I've recorded all the evidence given by people who came to my office, and there were no Serbs who reported to my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, it seems -- and reporting to your office, it seems that there were two ways that you garnered information. One was that people would come through your door to your office, and the second was that you actually went out on the ground, I believe, you said today in the transcript. When you went out on the ground -- well, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. When we went on the ground and when we came across cases of Serbs being injured, we were not allowed by the Serb police and military to get any close to that case because they did not recognise our council.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you were on the ground and going out to interview people, how did you select the interviewees?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: There was a representative of the ICG with us when we went out on the ground. And he was guiding us. And it was them who provided us with a form and the questions and the questionnaire. And on the basis of what was included in the questionnaire, we carried out the interviews. We identified the villages, and they helped us out in conducting these interviews. In the villages where we went, there were very few people remaining because the villages were burned down. But the people we met during those visits, we asked them and they told their story. The majority of the population of those villages were expelled from their own homes. They were sent to Albania, and they had not returned to their own villages because they had no home to stay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So the ICG was directing whom would be interviewed; is that correct? You are nodding yes?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you have specific names on a list when you went into a village, or did you randomly encounter the people who were still there?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: No. It was just people who we came across. And they were very few. And they felt they had been victimised, they were tortured, and their houses were burned down. Of the 84 villages in our municipality, more than 60 were burned, up to 90 per cent of them. So up to 90 per cent of the 60 villages were burned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I assume you are getting the statistics that you are giving now at this time from your organisation?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: No, it was the municipality that provided me with the details. We also got some statistics from Mother Teresa Association.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did the ICG give you any sort of training, or did anyone engage in any training before you went out and did these interviews?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. Days before we went out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What did that training involve?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, they were lawyers and they instructed us on the way -- how to conduct the interviews. Although, from our side, five or six were professionally lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you instructed to look for specific things?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: But the basis was the questionnaire, we were instructed to stick to the questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And this questionnaire, when you were filling in the questionnaire, which is what you did when you spoke with them; correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you filling it out verbatim or were you paraphrasing what the person was telling you?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: There were cases that we were literally writing what they were saying. Most of the things that we would put down was authentic. We would literally put down what they said; it was verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you said that you were --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: So we would note down the words of the witness as they said them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: On -- these were on handwritten forms; correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. It was handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall on these forms, having done so many of them, what were the questions that were asked?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. There were included all the crime categories. We mainly asked, Was your house burned down; have you been beaten up; have you been insulted; has any of your relatives been killed; anyone detained; anyone raped; have you been evicted from your home?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was the first question on the form "Are you ready to testify at The Hague Tribunal, yes or no?"

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And then they went on, as you said, to specify different crimes that they could discuss that they had been victims or witnesses of; correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, has your house been burned down; who evicted you, was it the police, was it the paramilitary, or the army. If it was the police, who were the police officers. So this is roughly what questions we put to them because so much time has passed and I cannot exactly remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's completely understandable. When it asked for the author of the crime, did it say, for example, the VJ, the police, the paramilitary, or civilian?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there any other options listed for perpetrators of the crime?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Let me think. We asked, When did you leave your village; when were you expelled; were your documents torn. Because most of the people who were sent to Albania, their identity cards and documents were taken away from them and burned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: So the document was burned in the eyes of all the people who were being sent across the border to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's okay. We have a lot to cover that's in your statement, obviously, so I just wanted to go step by step. And I was simply wondering if there were any other options other than those four listed as perpetrators of the crime, that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, you said earlier, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. So I take it that means that those four were the categories that could be checked in for that?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: I can't remember. But you have the questionnaire in front of you, so you may tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I don't actually have the questionnaire in front of me, that's the problem. That's why I'm asking you. I am --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Can bring it in tomorrow if you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That would be --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Of course I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm actually going from your testimony in the Milutinovic trial where you discussed the form, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. MS. MARIE O'LEARY: At page 1242, if anyone wanted the reference on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I was just going through it in that manner since I didn't have the form with me. But if you have it with you, you can bring it tomorrow and perhaps we can discuss that then. One more question then as far as in this vein right now: Do you know who drafted this form that you were using?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: I said it earlier, it's the ICG.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to move on to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems a very convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must adjourn for the night now, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, and we continue tomorrow, I believe, at 2.15; and we will therefore adjourn overnight. A Court Officer will assist you with further details, and we will look forward to the balance of your evidence tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of July, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
